'''''Gradshteyn and Ryzhik''''' ('''''GR''''') is the informal name of a comprehensive [[table of integrals]] originally compiled by the Russian mathematicians I. S. Gradshteyn and I. M. Ryzhik. Its full title today is '''''Table of Integrals, Series, and Products'''''.

Since its first publication in 1943, it was considerably expanded and it soon became a "classic" and highly regarded reference for mathematicians, scientists and engineers. After the deaths of the original authors, the work was maintained and further expanded by other editors.

At some stage a German and English dual-language translation became available, followed by Polish, English-only and Japanese versions. After several further editions, the Russian and German-English versions went out of print and have not been updated after [[the fall of the Iron Curtain]], but the English version is still being actively maintained and refined by new editors, and it has recently been retranslated back into Russian as well.

==Overview==
One of the valuable characteristics of ''Gradshteyn and Ryzhik'' compared to similar compilations is that most listed integrals are referenced. The literature list contains 92 main entries and 140 additional entries (in the eighth English edition). The integrals are classified by numbers, which haven't changed from the fourth Russian up to the seventh English edition (the numbering in older editions as well as in the eighth English edition is not fully compatible).
The book does not only contain the integrals, but also lists additional properties and related [[special function]]s.
It also includes tables for [[integral transform]]s.
Another advantage of ''Gradshteyn and Ryzhik'' compared to [[computer algebra system]]s is the fact that all special functions and constants used in the evaluation of the integrals are listed in a registry as well, thereby allowing reverse lookup of integrals based on special functions or constants.

On the downsides, ''Gradshteyn and Ryzhik'' has become known to contain a relatively high number of typographical errors even in newer editions, which has repeatedly led to the publication of extensive [[errata]] lists. Earlier English editions were also criticized for their poor translation of mathematical terms<ref name="RMT_85"/><ref name="REV_153_5"/><ref name="REV_209_1"/> and mediocre print quality.<ref name="RMT_85"/><ref name="REV_153_5"/><ref name="Wimp_1997_1"/><ref name="Wimp_1997_2"/>

==<span class="anchor" id="Gradshteyn"></span><span class="anchor" id="Ryzhik"></span><span class="anchor" id="Geronimus"></span><span class="anchor" id="Tseytlin"></span>History==
The work was originally compiled by the Russian mathematicians Iosif Moiseevich Ryzhik (Russian: {{lang|ru|Иосиф Моисеевич Рыжик}}, German: {{lang|de|Jossif Moissejewitsch Ryschik}})<ref name="Wolfram_2005"/><ref group="nb" name="Ryzhik_Bio"/> and Izrail Solomonovich Gradshteyn (Russian: {{lang|ru|Израиль Соломонович Градштейн}}, German: {{lang|de|Israil Solomonowitsch Gradstein}}).<ref name="Wolfram_2005"/><ref group="nb" name="Gradshteyn_Bio"/> While some contents were original, significant portions were collected from other previously existing integral tables like [[David Bierens de Haan]]'s ''{{lang|fr|[[Nouvelles tables d'intégrales définies]]}}'' (1867),<ref name="Wolfram_2005"/><ref name="Bierens_de_Haan_1867"/> [[Václav Jan Láska]]'s ''{{lang|de|Sammlung von Formeln der reinen und angewandten Mathematik}}'' (1888–1894)<ref name="Wolfram_2005"/><ref name="Laska_1888"/> or [[Edwin Plimpton Adams]]' and [[Richard Lionel Hippisley]]'s ''Smithsonian Mathematical Formulae and Tables of Elliptic Functions'' (1922).<ref name="Wolfram_2005"/><ref name="Adams_Hippisley_1922"/>

The [[#GR-R1|first]] edition, which contained about 5&thinsp;000 formulas,<ref name="RMT_219"/><ref name="ZBL_34-070"/><ref group="nb" name="Formula_Entry"/> was authored by Ryzhik,<ref group="nb" name="Ryzhik_Bio"/> who had already published a book on [[special function]]s in 1936<ref name="Wolfram_2005"/><ref name="Ryzhik_1936"/> and died during [[World War II]] around 1941.<ref name="Wolfram_2005"/> Not announcing this fact, his compilation was published posthumously<ref name="Wolfram_2005"/><ref group="nb" name="Ryzhik_Bio"/> in 1943, followed by a [[#GR-R2|second]] corrected edition in his name in 1948.<ref group="nb" name="NB_Death"/>

The [[#GR-R3|third]] edition (1951) was worked on by Gradshteyn,<ref name="Rosenfeld_2003"/> who also introduced the chapter numbering system in [[Decimal book chapter numbering|decimal notation]]. Gradshteyn planned considerable expansion for the fourth edition, a work he could not finish due to his own death.<ref name="Wolfram_2005"/><ref group="nb" name="Gradshteyn_Bio"/> Therefore, the [[#GR-R4|fourth]] (1962/1963) and [[#GR-R5|fifth]] (1971) editions were continued by [[Yuri Veniaminovich Geronimus]] (Russian: {{lang|ru|Юрий Вениаминович Геронимус}}, German: {{lang|de|Juri Weniaminowitsch Geronimus}})<ref name="Wolfram_2005"/><ref group="nb" name="Geronimus_Bio"/> and [[Michail Yulyevich Tseytlin]] (Russian: {{lang|ru|Михаил Ю́льевич Цейтлин}}, German: {{lang|de|Michael Juljewitsch Zeitlin}}).<ref group="nb" name="Tseytlin_Bio"/> The fourth edition contained about 12&thinsp;000 formulas already.<ref name="ZBL_103-038"/><ref group="nb" name="Formula_Entry"/>

Based on the third Russian edition, the [[#GR-G1|first]] German-English edition with 5&thinsp;400 formulas<ref name="RMT_69"/><ref group="nb" name="Formula_Entry"/> was published in 1957 by the East-German {{lang|de|[[Deutscher Verlag der Wissenschaften]]}} (DVW) with German translations by [[Christa Berg née Jahncke|Christa]]<ref group="nb" name="Berg_Ch_Bio"/> and [[Lothar Berg]]<ref group="nb" name="Berg_L_Bio"/> and the English texts by Martin Strauss.<ref group="nb" name="Strauss_Bio"/> In {{lang|de|[[Zentralblatt für Mathematik]]}} [[Karl Prachar]] wrote:<ref name="ZBL_80-337"/>

{{blockquote|"{{lang|de|Die sehr reichhaltigen Tafeln wurden nur aus dem Russischen ins Deutsche und Englische übersetzt.}}"<br />(Translation: The very comprehensive tables were only translated into German and English language.)}}

In 1963, it was followed by the [[#GR-G2|second]] edition, a reprint edition with a four-page inlet listing corrections compiled by [[Eldon Robert Hansen]].

Derived from the 1963 edition, but considerably expanded and split into two volumes, the [[#GR-G3|third]] German-English edition by [[Ludwig Boll]]<ref group="nb" name="Boll_Bio"/> was finally published by [[MIR Moscow]] in 1981 (with permission of DVW and distributed through [[Verlag Harri Deutsch]] in the Western world); it incorporated the material of the fifth Russian edition (1971) as well.<ref group="nb" name="Sixth_Russian"/>

Pending this third German-English edition an English-only edition by Alan Jeffrey<ref group="nb" name="Jeffrey_Bio"/> was published in 1965. Lacking a clear designation by itself it was variously known as [[#GR-E3|first, third<!-- as it followed the 2nd German-English edition and because this edition number fits in nicely after the publication of the (actually so called) fifth English edition in 1994 --> or fourth]] English edition, as it was based on the then-current fourth Russian edition. The formulas were photographically reproduced and the text translated. This still held true for the expanded [[#GR-E4|fourth]] English edition in 1980, which added chapters 10 to 17.<ref name="ZBL_521-193-1"/>

Both of these editions saw multiple [[print run]]s each incorporating newly found corrections. Starting with the third printing<!-- 1967 or 1969? -->, updated table entries were marked by adding a small superscript number to the entry number indicating the corresponding print run ("3" etc.<!-- print run "7" of 4th edition is documented for 1990 -->), a convention carried over into later editions by continuing to increase the superscript number as kind of a [[revision number]] (no longer directly corresponding with actual print runs).

The [[#GR-E5|fifth]] edition (1994), which contained close to 20&thinsp;000 formulas,<ref name="ZBL_918-65002"/><ref group="nb" name="Formula_Entry"/> was [[digital reset (typesetting)|electronically reset]]<ref name="REV_209_1"/> in preparation for a [[CD-ROM]] issue of the fifth edition (1996) and in anticipation of further editions. Since the [[#GR-E6|sixth]] edition (2000), now corresponding with superscript number "10", Daniel Zwillinger<ref group="nb" name="Zwillinger_Bio"/> started contributing as well. The last edition being edited by Jeffrey before his death<ref group="nb" name="Jeffrey_Bio"/> was the [[#GR-E7|seventh]] English edition published in 2007 (with superscript number "11").<ref name="Jeffrey_2007"/> This edition has been retranslated back into Russian as "[[#GR-R7|seventh]] Russian edition" in 2011.<ref name="APRU_2011"/><ref group="nb" name="Sixth_Russian"/>

For the [[#GR-E8|eighth]] edition (2014/2015, with superscript number "12") Zwillinger took over the role of the editor. He was assisted by [[Victor Hugo Moll]].<ref name="Zwillinger_2014"/><ref group="nb" name="Moll_Bio"/> In order to make room for additional information without increasing the size of the book significantly, the former chapters 11 (on [[algebraic inequality|algebraic inequalities]]), chapters 13 to 16 (on [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] and related results, [[determinant]]s, [[norm (mathematics)|norm]]s, [[ordinary differential equation]]s) and chapter 18 (on [[z-transform]]s) worth about 50 pages in total were removed and some chapters renumbered (12 to 11, 17 to 12). This edition contains more than 10&thinsp;000 entries.<ref name="Zwillinger_2014"/><ref group="nb" name="Formula_Entry"/>

==<span class="anchor" id="Handbook"></span><span class="anchor" id="Proofs"></span>Related projects==
In 1995, Alan Jeffrey published his ''Handbook of Mathematical Formulas and Integrals''.<ref name="Jeffrey_1995"/>
It was partially based on the fifth English edition of Gradshteyn and Ryzhik's ''Table of Integrals, Series, and Products'' and meant as a companion, but written to be more accessible for students and practitioners.<ref name="Jeffrey_1995"/> It went through four editions up to 2008.<ref name="Jeffrey_1995"/><ref name="Jeffrey_2000"/><ref name="Jeffrey_2003"/><ref name="Jeffrey_2008"/> The fourth edition also took advantage of changes incorporated into the seventh English edition of Gradshteyn and Ryzhik.<ref name="Jeffrey_2008"/>

Inspired by a 1988 paper in which {{ill|Ilan Vardi|de}} proved several integrals in ''Gradshteyn and Ryzhik'',<ref name="Vardi_1988"/> Victor Hugo Moll with George Boros started a project to prove all integrals listed in ''Gradshteyn and Ryzhik'' and add additional commentary and references.<ref name="Moll_2010"/> In the foreword of the book ''Irresistible Integrals'' (2004), they wrote:<ref name="Boros_2004"/>
{{blockquote|It took a short time to realize that this task was monumental.}}
Nevertheless, the efforts have meanwhile resulted in about 900<!-- count of entries in articles 1-30: 10+5+8+44+10+65+30+7+45+76+52+6+21+1+(12[-1])+36+36+(7[+3])+42+26+75+36+54+10+18+41+37+17+(19[+16])+51=897[+18] --> entries from ''Gradshteyn and Ryzhik'' discussed in a series of more than 30 articles<ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_29"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_30"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_X1"/> of which papers 1 to 28{{efn|<!-- <ref name="Moll_Paper_1"/> --><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_1"/><!-- <ref name="Moll_Paper_2"/> --><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_2"/><!-- <ref name="Moll_Paper_3"/> --><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_3"/><!-- <ref name="Moll_Paper_4"/> --><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_4"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_5"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_6"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_7"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_8"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_9"/><!-- <ref name="Moll_Paper_10"/> --><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_10"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_11"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_12"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_13"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_14"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_15"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_16"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_17"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_18"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_19"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_20"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_21"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_22"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_23"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_24"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_25"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_26"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_27"/><ref name="Moll_Scientia_Part_28"/>}} have been published in issues 14 to 26<!-- except for 24 --> of [[Scientia (UTFSM journal)|Scientia]], [[Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María]] (UTFSM), between 2007 and 2015<ref name="Moll_Scientia"/> and compiled into a two-volume book series ''Special Integrals of Gradshteyn and Ryzhik: the Proofs'' (2014–2015) already.<ref name="Moll_SIGR1_2014"/><ref name="Moll_SIGR2_2015"/>

{{reflist|group="nb"|refs=
{{r|group="nb"|name="Ryzhik_Bio"|r={{anchor|NB_Ryzhik_Bio}}[[Iosif Moiseevich Ryzhik]] ({{lang|ru|Иосиф Моисеевич Рыжик}})<ref name="Wolfram_2005"/> (1918?–1941?). {{VIAF|15286520}}. {{GND|107340518|1087809320}}.[https://books.google.com/books?id=fEGxAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA300][http://jmemory.org/memorial/R/r-6.htm<!-- https://web.archive.org/web/20180111234607/http://jmemory.org/memorial/R/r-6.htm -->] (NB. Some sources identify him as a [[sergeant]] ({{lang|ru|сержантом}}) born in 1918, originally from [[Vitebsk]] ({{lang|ru|Витебска}}), who was drafted into the army in 1939 from Chkalovsk ({{lang|ru|Чкаловска}}), Orenburg ({{lang|ru|Оренбург}}),<!-- source? or: Витебским ГВК/Vitebsk GVK--> and got missing in December 1941.[https://web.archive.org/web/20220115233308/http://mishpoha.org/martirolognew/672-martirolog-evrei-vitebska-pavshie-v-boyakh-s-natsizmom-v-1941-1945-gg<!-- Рыжик Иосиф Моисеевич Р. в 1918 в Витебске. Призв.: Витебским ГВК, сержант. Пропал без вести в декабре 1941. -->] However, since a birth year 1918 would have made him a very young author ([[#Ryzhik-1936|18]]), this could also have been a [[namesake]]. In the foreword of the first edition of the book, Ryzhik thanked three mathematicians of the [[Moscow Mathematical Society]] for their suggestions and advice: 
[[Vyacheslav Vassilievich Stepanov]] ({{lang|ru|Вячеслав Васильевич Степанов}}), [[Aleksei Ivanovich Markushevich]] ({{lang|ru|Алексей Иванович Маркушевич}}), and [[Ilya Nikolaevich Bronshtein]] ({{lang|ru|Илья Николаевич Бронштейн}}), suggesting that he must have been in some way associated with this group.)}}
{{r|group="nb"|name="Gradshteyn_Bio"|r=[[Izrail Solomonovich Gradshteyn]] ({{lang|ru|Израиль Соломонович Градштейн}})<!-- <ref name="Rosenfeld_2003"/><ref name="Wolfram_2005"/> --> (1899, Odessa – 1958, Moscow). {{VIAF|20405466}}, {{VIAF|310677818}}, {{VIAF|270418384}}. ISNI&nbsp;0000000116049405. {{GND|11526194X}}.}}
<ref group="nb" name="Formula_Entry">Following the sources, this article distinguishes between the documented number of ''formulas'' and the number of ''entries''.</ref>
<ref group="nb" name="NB_Death">The fact that Ryzhik's death was not announced before the [[#GR-R3|third]] edition of the book in 1951 might indicate that his status was unclear for a number of years, or, in the case of the [[#GR-R1|first]] edition, that [[hot lead typesetting|typesetting]] had already started, but actual production of the book had to be delayed and was then finalized in his absence as a consequence of the war.</ref>

It is unknown if any changes for the [[#GR-R5|fifth]] Russian edition (1971) or the [[#GR-G3|third]] German-English edition (1981), which ''did'' incorporate material from the fifth Russian edition, were reflected in any of the English editions in between (and thereby in the seventh Russian edition as well).</ref>

<ref name="Wolfram_2005">{{cite web |title=The History and Future of Special Functions |at=The story behind Gradshteyn-Ryzhik |author-first=Stephen |author-last=Wolfram |author-link=Stephen Wolfram |date=2005-10-08 |publisher=[[Stephen Wolfram, LLC]] |work=Wolfram Technology Conference, [[Festschrift]] for [[Oleg Marichev]], in honor of his 60th birthday |location=Champaign, IL, USA |type=speech, blog post |url=http://www.stephenwolfram.com/publications/history-future-special-functions/#GRbook |access-date=2016-04-06 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160407015353/http://www.stephenwolfram.com/publications/history-future-special-functions/#GRbook |archive-date=2016-04-07 |quote=[…] In 1936 Iosif Moiseevich Ryzhik had a book entitled ''[[#Ryzhik-1936|Special Functions]]'' published by the [[United Moscow-Leningrad Scientific-Technical Publisher]]. Ryzhik died in 1941, either during the [[siege of Leningrad]], or fighting on the Russian front. In 1943, a table of formulas was published under Ryzhik's name by the [[Governmental Moscow-Leningrad Technical-Theoretical Publisher]]. The only thing the book seems to say about its origins is that it's responding to the shortage of books of formulas. It says that some integrals marked in it are original, but the others mostly come from three books—[[#Bierens_de_Haan-1867|a French one]] from 1858, [[#Laska-1888|a German one]] from 1894, and [[#Adams_Hippisley-1922|an American one]] from 1922. It explains that effort went into the ordering of the integrals, and that some are simplified by using a new special function ''s'' equal to [[Gamma function|Gamma]][''x''+''y''-1]/(Gamma[''x'']Gamma[''y'']). It then thanks [[#NB_Ryzhik_Bio|three fairly prominent mathematicians]] from Moscow University. That's basically all we know about Ryzhik. […] Israil Solomonovitch Gradshteyn was born in 1899 in Odessa, and became a professor of mathematics at [[Moscow State University]]. But in 1948, he was fired as part of the [[Soviet attack on Jewish academics]]. To make money, he wanted to write a book. And so he decided to build on Ryzhik's tables. Apparently he never met Ryzhik. But he created a new edition, and by the third edition, the book was known as Gradshteyn-Ryzhik. […] Gradshteyn died of natural causes in Moscow in 1958. Though somehow there developed an urban legend that one of the authors of Gradshteyn-Ryzhik had been shot as a [[anti-cosmopolitan campaign|piece of anti-Semitism]] on the grounds that an error in their tables had caused an airplane crash. […] Meanwhile, starting around 1953, Yurii Geronimus, who had met Gradshteyn at Moscow State University, began helping with the editing of the tables, and actually added the appendices on special functions. Later on, several more people were involved. And when the tables were published in the West, there were arguments about royalties. But Geronimus [in 2005 was<!-- is now -->] still alive and well and living in Jerusalem, and [[Oleg Igorevich Marichev|Oleg]] phoned him<!-- last week --> […]}}</ref>
